notes.definition: Nuclear fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus. In this process some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation.
explanation: Nuclear fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus. For example, two isotopes of hydrogen, hydrogen-2 (deuterium) and hydrogen-3 (tritium), can fuse to form helium-4 and a neutron: ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n. As with all nuclear equations, the mass numbers (2 + 3 = 4 + 1) and atomic numbers (1 + 1 = 2 + 0) balance.

In fusion, the total mass of the products is slightly less than the total mass of the nuclei that fused. Some of the mass has been converted into energy, which is released as radiation (and as kinetic energy of the products). Although the mass lost in each reaction is tiny, the number of reactions is enormous, so fusion releases a huge amount of energy.

Fusion is the energy source of the Sun and other stars. In the core of the Sun, hydrogen nuclei fuse to make helium. The core is at a temperature of millions of degrees and the pressure is enormous. These conditions are needed because nuclei are positively charged and repel each other: they must be moving extremely fast and be squeezed close together before they can get close enough to fuse.

Fusion is different from fission. Fission splits a large, heavy nucleus (such as uranium) into two smaller nuclei; fusion joins two light nuclei (such as hydrogen) into one heavier nucleus. Both release energy. Fission is used in nuclear power stations today, but scientists have not yet built a fusion power station that releases more energy than it uses, because it is very hard to create and contain such high temperatures and pressures.

If fusion power can be made practical, it would have advantages: hydrogen isotopes are plentiful (deuterium can be extracted from seawater), fusion produces no carbon dioxide, and it produces much less long-lived radioactive waste than fission. Experimental reactors heat hydrogen to over 100 million °C and use strong magnetic fields to hold it away from the walls.
keyFacts: Nuclear fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus.
Some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation.
The mass of the products is slightly less than the mass of the original nuclei.
Fusion of hydrogen into helium is the energy source of the Sun and stars.
Very high temperatures and pressures are needed because nuclei are positive and repel each other.
Mass numbers and atomic numbers balance in fusion equations.
Fission splits heavy nuclei; fusion joins light nuclei.
Fusion power stations are not yet practical, because the conditions are hard to create and contain.

keyTerms.definition: The joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy.
A nucleus with a small mass number, such as an isotope of hydrogen or helium.
Hydrogen-2 (²₁H): an isotope of hydrogen with one proton and one neutron.
Hydrogen-3 (³₁H): an isotope of hydrogen with one proton and two neutrons.
The small decrease in total mass in a fusion reaction, which is released as energy of radiation.
The force pushing two positively charged nuclei apart, which must be overcome for fusion to occur.

workedExamples.title: Balancing a fusion equation
workedExamples.question: Complete the equation ²₁H + ²₁H → He + ¹₀n by finding the mass number and atomic number of the helium nucleus.
steps: Mass numbers: 2 + 2 = 4, so helium mass number = 4 − 1 = 3.
Atomic numbers: 1 + 1 = 2, so helium atomic number = 2 − 0 = 2.

workedExamples.title: Mass converted into energy
workedExamples.question: In one fusion reaction the total mass before (²₁H + ³₁H) is 8.3510 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and the total mass after (⁴₂He + ¹₀n) is 8.3196 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. Calculate the mass converted into energy.
steps: Mass converted = mass before − mass after.

workedExamples.title: Percentage of mass converted
workedExamples.question: Using the values above, calculate the percentage of the original mass converted into energy.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often confuse fusion with fission.
misconceptions.right: In fact fusion joins (fuses) light nuclei together; fission splits a heavy nucleus apart.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think mass is conserved exactly in fusion.
misconceptions.right: In fact the products have slightly less mass; that mass has been converted into energy.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think fusion happens easily, as it powers the Sun.
misconceptions.right: In fact it needs extremely high temperatures and pressures to overcome the repulsion between positive nuclei.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think fusion power stations are already supplying electricity.
misconceptions.right: In fact fusion is still experimental; current power stations use fission.

realWorld: The Sun converts about 4 million tonnes of mass into energy every second by fusing hydrogen into helium.
Experimental fusion reactors such as JET in the UK and ITER in France use magnetic fields to hold hot hydrogen plasma.
Hydrogen bombs use fusion reactions, started by the high temperatures of a fission explosion.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is in separate Physics (8463) only. It is not assessed in Combined Science Trilogy (8464).
examTips: Use the word 'join' for fusion and 'split' for fission so the examiner can see you know the difference.
When asked where the energy comes from, say some of the mass is converted into energy.
Explain the need for high temperature and pressure by referring to the repulsion between positive nuclei.
Balance fusion equations in the same way as other nuclear equations: top numbers and bottom numbers.
summary: Fusion joins two light nuclei into a heavier nucleus.
Some mass is converted into energy of radiation.
Fusion powers the Sun and stars.
Very high temperature and pressure are needed to overcome repulsion.
Fission splits heavy nuclei; fusion joins light nuclei.

questions.question: What is nuclear fusion?
options: Splitting a heavy nucleus into two
Joining two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus
A nucleus emitting a gamma ray
An electron moving between energy levels
markScheme: 1 mark: Joining two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus
questions.explanation: Fusion joins light nuclei. Splitting a heavy nucleus is fission.

questions.question: What is the main source of energy in the Sun?
markScheme: 1 mark: Nuclear fusion of hydrogen
questions.explanation: The Sun's energy comes from hydrogen nuclei fusing into helium. It is not chemical burning.

questions.question: Which nuclei are most commonly involved in fusion?
markScheme: 1 mark: Hydrogen isotopes
questions.explanation: Fusion joins light nuclei, such as isotopes of hydrogen. Uranium and plutonium are used in fission.

questions.question: In a fusion reaction, how does the total mass of the products compare with the total mass of the original nuclei?
markScheme: 1 mark: It is slightly less
questions.explanation: A small amount of mass is converted into energy, so the products have slightly less mass.

questions.question: Why are very high temperatures needed for fusion?
options: So the nuclei move fast enough to overcome their electrostatic repulsion
To produce neutrons for a chain reaction
markScheme: 1 mark: So the nuclei move fast enough to overcome their electrostatic repulsion
questions.explanation: Positive nuclei repel. Only at very high temperatures do they move fast enough to get close enough to fuse.

questions.question: Which equation shows a fusion reaction?
markScheme: 1 mark: ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n
questions.explanation: Two light hydrogen nuclei join to make heavier helium: fusion. The others are fission, alpha decay and beta decay.

questions.question: Why is it difficult to build a fusion power station?
options: Fusion produces large amounts of carbon dioxide
Very high temperatures and pressures are hard to create and contain
markScheme: 1 mark: Very high temperatures and pressures are hard to create and contain
questions.explanation: The extreme conditions needed are very difficult to produce and hold in a reactor. Hydrogen isotopes are plentiful, and fusion produces no carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Complete the fusion equation: ¹₁H + ²₁H → X + γ. What is X?
markScheme: 1 mark: ³₂He
questions.explanation: Mass numbers: 1 + 2 = 3. Atomic numbers: 1 + 1 = 2. Gamma has no mass or charge, so X = ³₂He.

questions.question: Which statement correctly compares fission and fusion?
options: Fission needs very high temperatures; fusion needs a neutron to be absorbed
Fission splits heavy nuclei and fusion joins light nuclei; both release energy
markScheme: 1 mark: Fission splits heavy nuclei and fusion joins light nuclei; both release energy
questions.explanation: Fission splits heavy nuclei, fusion joins light nuclei, and both release energy. Fusion, not fission, needs very high temperatures.

questions.question:
In the fusion reaction ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + X, X is a single particle with atomic number 0.
Calculate the mass number of X.
markScheme: 1 mark: 1
questions.explanation: Mass numbers: 2 + 3 = 5 = 4 + A, so A = 1. It is a neutron, ¹₀n.

questions.question:
Two hydrogen-2 nuclei fuse: ²₁H + ²₁H → ³₁H + X.
X is a single particle. Calculate the mass number of X.
markScheme: 1 mark: A = 1 (X is a proton, ¹₁H)
questions.explanation: Mass numbers: 4 = 3 + 1. Atomic numbers: 2 = 1 + 1, so X is a proton.

questions.question:
Two hydrogen-2 nuclei fuse: ²₁H + ²₁H → ³₂He + ¹₀n. The total mass before is 6.6872 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and the total mass after is 6.6813 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
Calculate the mass converted into energy, in units of 10⁻²⁷ kg.
questions.explanation: Mass converted = mass before − mass after.

questions.question:
In the Sun, four hydrogen nuclei (total mass 6.6904 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) eventually form one helium nucleus (mass 6.6447 × 10⁻²⁷ kg).
Calculate the percentage of the original mass converted into energy. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
markScheme: 1 mark: mass converted = 0.0457 × 10⁻²⁷ kg
questions.explanation: Only a tiny fraction (under 1%) of the mass becomes energy, yet this powers the Sun.

questions.question:
The Sun converts about 4.0 × 10⁹ kg of mass into energy every second.
Calculate the mass converted into energy in one minute.
markScheme: 1 mark: 2.4 × 10¹¹ kg
questions.explanation: Multiply the rate by the time: 60 s × 4.0 × 10⁹ kg/s = 2.4 × 10¹¹ kg.

questions.question: State what is meant by nuclear fusion.
markScheme: 1 mark: the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus
questions.explanation: Fusion means joining together.

questions.question: Name the element whose nuclei fuse in the Sun.
markScheme: 1 mark: hydrogen
questions.explanation: Hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium.

questions.question: Explain where the energy released in a fusion reaction comes from.
markScheme: 1 mark: the products have slightly less mass than the original nuclei
1 mark: this mass is converted into energy (of radiation)
questions.explanation: Mass is not conserved exactly; the lost mass becomes energy.

questions.question: Explain why very high temperatures and pressures are needed for fusion.
markScheme: 1 mark: nuclei are positively charged so they repel each other
1 mark: high temperature makes them move fast enough (and high pressure pushes them close enough) to fuse
questions.explanation: Both conditions help overcome the repulsion between nuclei.

questions.question: Give two differences between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion.
acceptedAnswers: fission heavy nuclei fusion light nuclei
markScheme: 1 mark: fission splits a nucleus; fusion joins nuclei
1 mark: fission uses heavy nuclei (uranium/plutonium); fusion uses light nuclei (hydrogen) / fusion needs very high temperature and pressure / fission used in power stations, fusion not yet
questions.explanation: Each difference should refer to both processes.

questions.question: Suggest two advantages of generating electricity using fusion rather than fission, and one reason why this is not yet done.
markScheme: 1 mark: fuel (hydrogen isotopes) is plentiful, e.g. from seawater
1 mark: produces less long-lived radioactive waste / no carbon dioxide
1 mark: very high temperatures and pressures are hard to create and contain / uses more energy than it releases so far
questions.explanation: Fusion promises clean, plentiful energy but is technically very difficult.

questions.question: Explain why fusion does not happen at room temperature even though hydrogen nuclei are close together in hydrogen gas.
markScheme: 1 mark: nuclei are positively charged and repel each other
1 mark: at room temperature they do not move fast enough to get close enough to fuse
questions.explanation: Only at millions of degrees do nuclei move fast enough to overcome repulsion.

questions.question: What is released in a fusion reaction?
markScheme: 1 mark: Energy
questions.explanation: Fusion releases energy, because some mass is converted into energy of radiation.

questions.question: Hydrogen-2 and hydrogen-3 are used as fuel in experimental fusion reactors. What are they?
options: Different elements with the same mass number
Isotopes of hydrogen with 1 and 2 neutrons
Isotopes of hydrogen with 2 and 3 protons
markScheme: 1 mark: Isotopes of hydrogen with 1 and 2 neutrons
questions.explanation: Both have 1 proton (they are hydrogen). Hydrogen-2 has 1 neutron and hydrogen-3 has 2 neutrons.

questions.question: Name the heavier element formed when hydrogen nuclei fuse in the Sun.
markScheme: 1 mark: helium
questions.explanation: Hydrogen nuclei fuse, eventually forming helium.

questions.question: Describe the process of nuclear fusion and explain why it releases energy. Include an example.
markScheme: Indicative content: two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus; example: hydrogen-2 + hydrogen-3 → helium-4 + neutron, or hydrogen to helium in the Sun; mass of products slightly less than mass before; mass converted into energy of radiation; needs very high temperature and pressure to overcome repulsion between positive nuclei.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear description with an example and a correct explanation of the energy release.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): a basic definition or example with little explanation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Link the energy release to the loss of mass.

questions.question: Compare nuclear fission and nuclear fusion as ways of releasing energy. Include the nuclei involved, the conditions needed, how energy is released and their use for generating electricity.
markScheme: Indicative content: fission splits large unstable nuclei (uranium-235, plutonium-239) into two smaller nuclei; usually needs neutron absorption; releases 2 or 3 neutrons and gamma rays, chain reaction; controlled in reactors with control rods; used in power stations now; produces long-lived radioactive waste; fusion joins light nuclei (hydrogen isotopes) to form heavier nuclei; needs very high temperature and pressure to overcome repulsion; some mass converted into energy of radiation; powers the Sun; plentiful fuel, little long-lived waste; not yet practical for electricity because conditions are hard to create and contain; both release large energy per kg compared with chemical fuels.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed comparison across all four aspects with clear similarities and differences.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): compares fission and fusion in at least two aspects correctly.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple descriptions of one or both processes with little comparison.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Organise by aspect (nuclei, conditions, energy, use), stating both processes each time.
